title: Cyberchondriacs
paragraphs: How are you feeling today? I've got a few aches and pains but nothing serious. However, when things become more critical I would normally book myself an appointment with my GP — although by the time I get to see him, the problem will have probably gone away. That's because in the UK at least, we usually have to wait a few days before the doctor can fit us in and then when we're at the surgery, we have a long wait.

Luckily today, technology has come to our rescue. There are thousands of apps available on our smartphones that can offer first aid advice and allow us to self-diagnose our ailments — ranging from a simple cold or flu to some exotic disease such as dengue fever. And together with the internet, we have a whole encyclopedia of medical information at our fingertips.

But is this just what the doctor ordered? Is too much knowledge a good thing? By reading up on an illness, we discover its side-effects and what could happen in a worst-case situation. More worrying is that we give ourselves the wrong diagnosis, and then worry ourselves sick that we're going to die. This health anxiety fuelled by the internet, is called cyberchondria. It gives sufferers a deep fear of diseases and, according to experts, it's on the rise. Professor Peter Tyrer from Imperial College London, told the BBC: "We find that approximately four out of five of our patients with health anxiety spend literally hours on the internet.... one of the first things we do in treatment is we tell them to stop browsing the internet."

Of course there is no doubt, the world wide web has most of the information we need to diagnose our symptoms but Doctor Tyrer points out "it doesn't have any judgement associated with it." This is why having a consultation with a doctor face-to-face still has its benefits, although a study a few years ago found many GPs felt intimidated by the increasing numbers of web-wise patients arriving in surgeries. One doctor admitted to not being very happy about patients using the internet, saying: "They all seemed to come to me with things I'd never heard of and very often with things which seem rather bizarre or inappropriate."

But Professor Sue Ziebland, from Oxford University, has spent 15 years examining how patients use the internet - including people with cancer. She found that doctors now routinely discuss it as a resource with patients during consultations so it becomes an everyday part of medical conversation. It would seem then that a virtual online doctor can prescribe a dose of useful advice but technology hasn't replaced the human medical expert just yet.

vocabulary.entry: aches and pains [phr.] /eɪks ənd peɪnz/ 疼痛不适 (口语)
vocabulary.example: After the long hike, I had aches and pains all over my body.
vocabulary.translation: 长途徒步后，我浑身疼痛不适。

vocabulary.entry: critical [adj.] /ˈkrɪtɪkəl/ 危急的；关键的 (书面语)
vocabulary.example: The patient is in critical condition after the accident.
vocabulary.translation: 事故后病人情况危急。

vocabulary.entry: fit us in [phr.] /fɪt əs ɪn/ 安排时间见我们 (口语)
vocabulary.example: The doctor can fit you in at 4 o‘clock this afternoon.
vocabulary.translation: 医生可以在今天下午4点安排时间见你。

vocabulary.entry: self-diagnose [v.] /ˌself ˈdaɪəɡnəʊz/ 自我诊断 (专业词汇)
vocabulary.example: It’s dangerous to self-diagnose your symptoms using the internet.
vocabulary.translation: 用互联网自我诊断症状是危险的。

vocabulary.entry: ailments [n. pl.] /ˈeɪlmənts/ 疾病；小毛病 (书面语；单数: ailment)
vocabulary.example: The clinic treats minor ailments like colds and headaches.
vocabulary.translation: 这家诊所治疗感冒和头痛等小毛病。

vocabulary.entry: fingertips [n. pl.] /ˈfɪŋɡətɪps/ 指尖；at one‘s fingertips 触手可及
vocabulary.example: With a smartphone, we have information at our fingertips.
vocabulary.translation: 有了智能手机，信息触手可及。

vocabulary.entry: fuelled by [phr.] /ˈfjuːəld baɪ/ 由……推动；由……引发 (书面语)
vocabulary.example: His anger was fuelled by jealousy.
vocabulary.translation: 他的愤怒是由嫉妒引发的。

vocabulary.entry: cyberchondria [n.] /ˌsaɪbəˈkɒndriə/ 网络疑病症 (专业词汇；新词)
vocabulary.example: Cyberchondria affects people who constantly search for health information online.
vocabulary.translation: 网络疑病症影响着那些不断在网上搜索健康信息的人。

vocabulary.entry: judgement [n.] /ˈdʒʌdʒmənt/ 判断力；判断 (书面语)
vocabulary.example: Using the internet for medical advice lacks professional judgement.
vocabulary.translation: 使用互联网获取医疗建议缺乏专业判断力。

vocabulary.entry: intimidated [adj.] /ɪnˈtɪmɪdeɪtɪd/ 害怕的；感到不安的
vocabulary.example: Some doctors feel intimidated by patients who research their symptoms online.
vocabulary.translation: 有些医生对在网上研究自己症状的病人感到不安。

vocabulary.entry: bizarre [adj.] /bɪˈzɑː/ 奇怪的；奇异的 (书面语)
vocabulary.example: He told a bizarre story about meeting an alien.
vocabulary.translation: 他讲了一个关于遇到外星人的奇怪故事。

vocabulary.entry: prescribe [v.] /prɪˈskraɪb/ 开（药）；给……开处方 (专业词汇)
vocabulary.example: The doctor prescribed antibiotics for the infection.
vocabulary.translation: 医生为感染开了抗生素。

vocabulary.entry: come to one‘s rescue [phr.] /kʌm tə wʌnz ˈreskjuː/ 救援某人；帮助某人
vocabulary.example: When the car broke down, a mechanic came to our rescue.
vocabulary.translation: 汽车抛锚时，一位机械师来帮助我们。

vocabulary.entry: first aid [n.] /ˌfɜːst ˈeɪd/ 急救 (专业词汇)
vocabulary.example: She took a first aid course to learn how to help in emergencies.
vocabulary.translation: 她参加了一个急救课程，学习如何在紧急情况下提供帮助。

vocabulary.entry: range from...to... [phr.] /reɪndʒ frɒm tuː/ 从……到……的范围
vocabulary.example: Her duties range from answering phones to managing the budget.
vocabulary.translation: 她的职责范围从接电话到管理预算。

vocabulary.entry: read up on [phr.] /riːd ʌp ɒn/ 查阅；研读
vocabulary.example: I need to read up on the topic before the presentation.
vocabulary.translation: 在做演示之前我需要查阅这个主题的资料。

vocabulary.entry: worry oneself sick [phr.] /ˈwʌri wʌnˈself sɪk/ 担心得要命 (口语)
vocabulary.example: She worried herself sick waiting for the test results.
vocabulary.translation: 她在等待测试结果时担心得要命。

vocabulary.entry: on the rise [phr.] /ɒn ðə raɪz/ 在增加；在增长
vocabulary.example: House prices are on the rise again.
vocabulary.translation: 房价又在上涨了。

vocabulary.entry: point out [phr.] /pɔɪnt aʊt/ 指出；说明
vocabulary.example: He pointed out the mistake in the report.
vocabulary.translation: 他指出了报告中的错误。

vocabulary.entry: routinely [adv.] /ruːˈtiːnli/ 例行地；常规地
vocabulary.example: The equipment is routinely checked for safety.
vocabulary.translation: 设备定期进行安全检查。

sentences.chinese: 更令人担忧的是，我们会给自己做出错误的诊断，然后担心自己会病死。

sentences.chinese: 这种由互联网加剧产生的健康焦虑被称为“网络疑病症”。

sentences.chinese: 当然，毫无疑问，万维网拥有我们诊断症状所需的大部分信息，但泰勒医生指出：“它没有任何相关的判断力。”

sentences.english: But Professor Sue Ziebland, from Oxford University, has spent 15 years examining how patients use the internet - including people with cancer.
sentences.chinese: 但是牛津大学的苏·齐布兰德教授花了15年时间研究患者如何使用互联网，包括癌症患者。

sentences.chinese: 她发现，医生现在在会诊时，会经常地与患者讨论互联网作为一种信息来源的问题，所以它已经成为医疗对话中日常的一部分。
